title: Cited conversational tax research in place of keyword database search
problem: Advisers pay for research databases but find them slow, and general chatbots return confident citations that may not exist.
approach: The adviser asks in plain language and gets an answer citing primary authority from a curated set (Blue J, Accordance, CoCounsel Tax).
A 25-person firm reports research falling from 1 hour to 10 minutes (vendor-published); Blue J says user disagreement is below 0.2% (vendor-published).
The adviser reads each cited authority before relying on it; a manager or partner tests the reasoning.
who: Blue J, Accordance, CoCounsel, RSM US, others

title: Multi-step research plans for gray-area tax questions
problem: Hard gray-area questions took hours across several databases, and applying findings to a client's situation still took substantial manual effort.
approach: The tool works in steps: extract facts, frame issues, locate authority, weigh relevance, recommend; Accordance, Bloomberg Tax and Thomson Reuters offer versions.
A CPA at a 100-professional firm says research taking 2-6 hours takes 15-20 minutes (vendor-published).
A senior researcher checks the plan, conclusions and authority; a partner reviews before advice goes to the client.

title: Research agent works a tax question end to end with cited answer
problem: Corporate tax research needs several chained lookups, and an early error in a threshold, date or citation carries through to the answer.
approach: An agent with lookup, search and calculator tools researches over many steps and submits a cited answer; EY India announced research agents.
Vals AI's independent benchmark top score was 49.19% (independent; models run in Vals harness, not a firm deployment).
A qualified adviser reviews the memo and every authority; scope phases from summarisation to position drafting only after verification.

title: Idea: specialist multi-state and multi-country tax research workflow
problem: Idea, not a deployment: multi-jurisdiction questions, such as 50-state surveys, are where tools do worst and manual work is longest.
approach: Idea: a purpose-built workflow searches each jurisdiction's primary law and compiles a comparison table for adviser review.
Vals suggests a specialist workflow should beat basic prompts; an adjacent legal study found AI scored 14 points lower on multi-jurisdiction questions.
The adviser verifies each jurisdiction's result against primary law.

title: Knowledge assistant over a firm's own memos, precedents and guidance
problem: Institutional tax knowledge sits in senior practitioners' heads and scattered memos; vendors say it is lost as seniors retire and quality varies.
approach: An assistant answers from the organisation's own memo library and policies alongside licensed content so staff reuse prior positions consistently.
Thomson Reuters markets CoCounsel Tax for in-house teams with a Knowledge Base; KPMG's knowledge management leader joined a panel. No outcomes.
The reviewer confirms a retrieved precedent still reflects current law and fits the client's facts.

title: In-house tax teams triage technical questions with licensed and enterprise AI
problem: Corporate tax teams answer ad hoc technical questions with limited staff; Thomson Reuters' 2025 survey found 58% of departments under-resourced.
approach: In KPMG Germany's quick surveys, 89% use company-wide AI solutions and 29% specialised tax applications (base not stated).
TEI's preliminary Midyear 2026 programme scheduled labs on AI tax research with Thomson Reuters CoCounsel and Accordance.
Tax director reviews AI-assisted conclusions before they go to the CFO, auditors or authorities.

title: Firm-wide standard on approved research assistants with a named tax AI owner
problem: Staff use general chatbots for tax questions whether or not approved, and large firms have uneven tools and no central control over what is pasted into AI.
approach: Crowe signed an enterprise agreement for Ask Blue J and has a Tax AI Leader; KPMG US M&A Tax built its own.
PwC has a US AI Tax Leader, a governance committee, over 3,200 AI champions, 800 custom GPTs and 250 agents (self-reported).
The managing partner or tax leader approves tools and keeps the approved list; human review applies at each level.
who: Crowe, KPMG US, PwC, Wright Ford Young

title: AI-supported research training and coaching for junior staff
problem: Junior staff lack the background to navigate legacy research tools, and seniors act as informal research trainers.
approach: Firms use the cited research assistant as a tutor; Jansen & Company's senior managing director says he uses AI as a tutor.
Sasserath & Co. says younger staff avoided unlearning legacy methods; Finney Neill says less experienced staff could not reach answers before.
A supervisor reviews juniors' research and reasoning, not only the answer.
who: Jansen & Company, Sasserath & Co., Finney Neill

title: Reusable planning blueprints turning client data into a decision matrix
problem: An S-corporation election analysis for a sole proprietor was about a 10-hour project, and research on the firm's old platform limited proactive client service.
approach: The firm builds a standard process (a blueprint) that takes client financials, researches the rules and produces a decision matrix.
A tax shareholder says a 10-hour project becomes roughly two to two and a half hours (vendor-published).
The tax shareholder reviews the matrix and localised assumptions before it goes to the client.

title: Idea: AI planning-alternative ideation and anti-abuse screening of structures
problem: Idea, not a deployment: finding and testing planning alternatives across a large body of authority is slow and depends on a few senior people.
approach: Idea: a model proposes or completes planning strategies and probes them against authority; the adviser decides whether any is supportable.
Blair-Stanek and colleagues report LLM reasoning identified an apparently novel strategy (independent; no rate or count). No adviser-use result published.
A senior adviser tests every AI-proposed structure against economic substance and professional standards.

title: Idea: AI challenges a tax position by arguing the other side
problem: Idea, not a deployment: positions are often tested only by the author and one reviewer, and a single tool's confident answer can be wrong.
approach: Idea: the adviser asks a model to argue the opposite, list what an IRS examiner would flag, or cross-checks a second tool.
Disagreement between tools triggers a deeper human check; CPA Practice Advisor's playbook suggests similar prompts for clients.
The adviser decides which objections are credible, checks material points against primary authority and updates the memo.

title: Auditable tax computation: AI translates rules, a calculation engine does the arithmetic
problem: Advice often turns on a computation, and language models alone get these wrong in ways that are hard to see.
approach: The model translates rules or facts into formal logic or inputs for a solver or tax engine; the logic trace is kept.
Johns Hopkins researchers tested this on a statutory reasoning dataset; best model computing 2024 returns scored 32.35% strict, 51.96% lenient (vendor-published).
The adviser reviews inputs, assumptions and the explanation of the calculation.

title: Document-grounded tax analysis of agreements, trusts and schedules
problem: Advisers read long operating agreements, trust and will documents and supporting schedules by hand before they can apply the tax rules.
approach: The adviser uploads a document; the tool summarises it and checks authority. Wright Ford Young uses it to review operating agreements.
Jansen & Company says it wants to analyse trust and will documents; Thomson Reuters describes schedule uploads. No outcomes published.
The adviser checks the summary against the source document before relying on it.
who: Wright Ford Young, Jansen & Company, Thomson Reuters

title: Drafting technical memos, advice letters and client emails from researched authority
problem: Writing the memo, advice letter or client explanation after research takes days of associate time, delays the response and varies between staff.
approach: The tool turns facts and authorities into a first draft the adviser edits and owns; Larson Gross uses Blue J.
KPMG describes a Writing Review Assistant; Lowy says output resembles an average junior associate's, useful for drafts but not ready to send.
A named adviser edits, verifies every cited authority and approves each client-facing draft; opinion-level documents get a second reviewer.
who: Blue J, Larson Gross, KPMG, Nelson Mullins

title: Idea: AI support for tax opinions and in-house preliminary positions
problem: Idea, not a deployment: written advice must rest on reasonable assumptions, and corporates often wait for an expensive Big Four or law-firm opinion.
approach: Idea: AI assembles authorities, maps them to facts and drafts the analysis; a person decides the conclusion and signs.
Kilpatrick Townsend says AI can help produce an opinion letter if the practitioner verifies analysis and replaces fabricated authorities.
The signing professional owns the conclusion; opinion committee or second-partner review still applies.

title: Answering client questions during the call instead of calling back
problem: Complex client questions meant saying 'we'll do some research and call you back', because research could consume most of a workday.
approach: With a cited research assistant open, the adviser looks up and tests an answer while the client is on the line.
A Barnes Wendling director says the team can now get answers on a phone call; 700+ queries per month tracked firm-wide (vendor-published).
The adviser decides what can be said live and what needs follow-up review.

title: Idea: client-facing tax question assistant that escalates to an adviser
problem: Idea, not a deployment: clients and self-preparers ask routine tax questions that consume adviser time, and many already ask general chatbots.
approach: Idea: a chatbot answers routine questions from the firm's approved content and routes nuanced or high-stakes ones to an adviser.
HMRC's guidelines for tax software using generative AI ask for flags on nuanced rules; no firm-deployed assistant outcome published.
Fact-dependent or advice-level questions escalate to a qualified adviser.

title: Idea: triage of AI-generated tax answers and citations that others bring
problem: Idea, not a deployment: clients ask a chatbot first, and counterparties send positions and citations that may be AI-generated and wrong.
approach: Idea: run incoming material through the citation checks used on the firm's own work, and counsel clients to ask AI for sources.
In Clinco the IRS flagged the nonexistent cases; in Harber the tribunal and HMRC found nine cited decisions did not exist.
The adviser reviews flagged material and its sources before adopting any position or responding.

title: Citation verification and an AI-use record as a standing review step
problem: AI can produce plausible but nonexistent authority; in Clinco three of four cited cases were described as probable AI hallucinations.
approach: Reviewers confirm every cited authority exists and supports the claim, and the file records prompt, output, citations, verification and reviewer.
KPMG US M&A Tax uses citations and hyperlinks to validate all AI outputs; Aon and Wolters Kluwer advise similar records.
2,199 decisions worldwide address hallucinated content (independent, 16 Oct 2026). A second reviewer cross-checks; the responsible partner signs off.
who: KPMG US, Aon adviser, Wolters Kluwer, Tax Court

title: Automated check that every cited authority exists and supports the point
problem: Fabricated or misdescribed citations reach client memos and court filings, and manual cite-checking of every authority is slow.
approach: A checker resolves every citation in a draft against authoritative sources and flags those that do not exist or support the point.
Damien Charlotin, who runs a hallucination-decisions database, offers an automated reference checker (PelAIkan); no tax error rates published (announced).
A person clears every flagged citation and reads the authorities that carry the argument.

title: M&A tax diligence: AI review of purchase agreements and a first-draft report
problem: Transaction tax teams read long purchase agreements, research deal rules and write diligence reports under deadlines, leaving less time for structuring and hidden-risk analysis.
approach: KPMG US M&A Tax describes four GenAI tools: research, agreement review against baselines, draft diligence reporting and a writing review assistant.
KPMG's web page says the firm is compressing weeks of tax analysis into minutes (self-reported).
Professionals add their own assessments and validate output against source documents; a senior reviewer signs the report.
who: KPMG US, a Hungarian advisory firm

title: Diligence agent reads data room and drafts cited tax risk assessment
problem: Tax diligence over entity structures, intercompany agreements and filings takes weeks of document analysis across entities and jurisdictions.
approach: V7 markets an agent that ingests financial statements, returns and agreements, maps entities, flags permanent establishment issues and returns a cited assessment.
V7's demo project compares 3-4 weeks to 2-3 days, 'average time saved 90%' (vendor-published).
The deal tax lead reviews the assessment before it informs price, structure or counterparty discussions.

title: Law-change monitoring that drafts client impact notes for adviser review
problem: After major legislation advisers must track guidance across jurisdictions and explain the effect to each client, which is repetitive and urgent.
approach: A monitoring agent watches new law and drafts client impact notes. KPMG US says building one went from weeks to minutes (self-reported).
Bloomberg Tax describes an AI Assistant in its Compliance Tracker; best model scored 66.67% on an independent law-change benchmark category (a proxy).
The adviser confirms each flagged change and its client impact before anything reaches the client.

title: Advisers co-build client-specific tax agents with clients on firm platforms
problem: KPMG's US tax vice chair says building an agent to help clients adjust to changing tax regulations used to take weeks and several tools.
approach: KPMG's Digital Gateway Powered by Claude, announced 20 May 2026, lets professionals and clients build agentic workflows, starting with tax.
EY announced EY.ai Tax Labs and the Tax Agent Factory (25 Nov 2025) to build and manage agents with clients.
KPMG US says weeks became minutes (self-reported). Human checkpoints are not described in the sources.

title: Value-based and fixed-fee pricing as AI shortens research and drafting
problem: Hourly billing ties revenue to time AI removes, and the IRS says billing for manual time not actually spent may violate the fee rule.
approach: Firms test fixed, hybrid or value-based fees; Sasserath & Co. moved onboarding to fixed monthly fees. A pricing change, not AI workflow.
RKL is piloting an alternative model and reports several dozen clients onboarded under it (self-reported).
The engagement partner sets the fee basis and reviews billing against actual work and the IRS fee rule.
who: Sasserath & Co., RKL, RSM US, PwC
